posts.text:
Wow, Largan Chairman dropped a nuke and stated MicroLEDs unlikely to become viable for AI DC buildouts

As for what's up and coming... Feels like $AMD, $NVDA, and everyone in the industry is clearly going out of their way to procure CW laser supply this year. 

EML was the market's focus last year with $LITE / $COHR (and still partially is). 

But future architectures with microleds was something to keep watch for 2028 onwards... 

Since $CRDO was pretty focused on it with their acqusition of Hyperlume, $AMS Osram was a popular name (working with Credo too), hyperscalers like $MSFT were developing in the space too. 

Largan is also a $TSM COUPE supply chain player that does FAU like Foci/microlens/passive components, so they're more impartial.

But yeah... was a surprise to see Largan Chairman citing concerns over "power consumption, size, and transmission efficiency" for microled commercialization and said it's unlikely to become viable. (source: Digitimes)

TLDR:
-> MicroLED as a technology unlikely to become viable from Largan Chairman
-> If it turns out correct, indirectly positive for lasers like VCSEL, then CW/SiPH since there's some overlap for CPO scale up applications

Nominal growth (inflation PLUS real growth) determines the proper level of NOMINAL yields. This means real growth has a role in setting NOMINAL yields.

NOMINAL yields are more than a reaction to inflation expectations, as I explained here.

https://x.com/biancoresearch/status/2107179794563531068?s=20

quoted.text:
I'm increasingly partial to the argument that increases in the fed funds rate will do little to lower inflation, and may be counterproductive. 
 - AI investment is unlikely to slow because interest rates are slightly higher
 - Energy is highly inelastic and rate changes can't alleviate the current supply shock
 - Higher rates hurt supply-side solutions in housing, energy, autos, and other capital intensive industries
 - Higher borrowing costs raise business operating expenses, some of which is passed along to consumers
 - A large percentage of debt is fixed-rate, dampening the feedback loop but hurting new homeowners, small businesses, and investment
 - An economy increasingly dominated by services is less sensitive to rate changes
 - This century has repeatedly demonstrated how blunt interest rate policy can be, both in stimulating inflation when it's low and suppressing it when it's high
